title: Blind Spot
desc: With one eye closed, the child stares at a cross on a card and moves it toward their face until a dot disappears, finding the eye's blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina.
how: Needs only a card and a ruler; a quick 10-minute surprise to start a lesson on the eye.

title: Sound Sandwich
desc: The child builds a harmonica-like noisemaker from two craft sticks, a rubber band and bits of straw, then blows through it and hears the pitch change as the straws are moved closer together.
how: Ice-cream sticks and rubber bands work fine; let children predict how the sound will change before moving the straws.

title: Bee Hummer
desc: The child makes a spinning toy from a popsicle stick, string and a wide rubber band; whirled around overhead, it buzzes like a swarm of bees as the band vibrates.
how: Do it outdoors with space to swing; ask why the buzz changes with speed.

title: Holding Charge
desc: The child rubs a plastic straw with its paper wrapper until it is charged, then sticks it to a wall or hand, makes two charged straws push apart and uses one to lift bits of paper or salt.
how: Works best on a dry day, so it suits winter more than the monsoon.

title: Flying Tinsel
desc: Using a pie pan charged with static electricity, the child makes a loop of tinsel float in the air, pushed away by electrostatic repulsion.
how: A follow-on to the straw or balloon static activities once the child knows charges can attract and repel.

title: Charge and Carry
desc: The child rubs a foam plate with wool to build up static charge and carries it to make a small, safe spark, then can check the charge with an electroscope.
how: Good for talking about lightning and why static sparks are small but real electricity.

title: Electroscope
desc: The child builds a simple electroscope from drinking straws and uses it to detect whether objects carry an electric charge.
how: Pair with Holding Charge or Charge and Carry to test which rubbed materials get charged.

title: Pinhole Magnifier
desc: The child looks at tiny print through a pinhole in a card and sees it look bigger, discovering that a smaller hole gives a sharper but dimmer image.
how: Needs only card and a pin; try holes of different sizes.

title: Poking Fun at Light Rays
desc: The child builds a simple pinhole viewer and sees an upside-down image of a bright object, learning that light travels in straight lines through the hole.
how: Use a bright window or a bulb in a dim room; ask why the image is upside down.

title: Fog Chamber
desc: In a jar sealed with a glove, the child pulls the glove outward to expand and cool the air and watches fog form on smoke particles, a cloud in a jar.
how: An adult must handle the lit match used to add smoke.

title: Pop Bottle
desc: The child twists a capped plastic water bottle tight, then pops the cap off and sees a small cloud of mist appear at the mouth as the air expands and cools.
how: Uses an empty water bottle; links neatly to how clouds form in the water cycle.

title: Seed Germinator
desc: The child lines a clear case with damp paper towel, places seeds along a line, stands it upright in water and checks daily as roots and then shoots emerge, measuring their growth.
how: Moong, chana or rajma seeds work well; keep a daily drawing or measurement log.

title: See Inside a Seed
desc: The child soaks beans, peels off the seed coat and splits them open to find the tiny root (radicle) and the cotyledons that feed the young plant.
how: Soak rajma or chana overnight; pairs well with Seed Germinator.

title: Vegetable Revival
desc: The child regrows new plants from leftover vegetable scraps and watches fresh shoots appear.
how: Kitchen scraps such as spring onion or coriander roots are ideal.

title: Magnetic Lines of Force
desc: The child holds a magnet against a sealed bottle of iron filings and sees the filings line up to show the magnet's field in three dimensions, without any mess.
how: Keep the bottle sealed with tape so filings stay inside.

title: Magnetic Shielding
desc: Paper clips hang from a magnet through layers of cardboard; when the child slides a pair of steel scissors between the layers and closes them, the clips drop off.
how: Ask which materials block the magnet and which let it through.

title: Where's North?
desc: The child hangs ring magnets on a thread and watches them line up with Earth's magnetic field, and sees like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

title: Eclipse in a Cup
desc: Using cups and a clay Moon, the child models the Moon's tilted orbit around Earth to see why eclipses do not happen every month.
how: Use before or after a solar or lunar eclipse visible from India.

title: Ocean Acidification in a Cup
desc: The child makes a purple red-cabbage indicator, then lets carbon dioxide from baking soda and vinegar dissolve into it and watches the surface turn pink as it becomes more acidic.
how: Red cabbage, baking soda and vinegar are easy to find; an adult should handle the hot water.

title: Time to Spring Clean…Your Water!
desc: The child makes muddy water and builds filters from plastic bottles, coffee filters and uncooked rice or beans, comparing how clean each makes the water.
how: Stress that filtered water may look clean but is not safe to drink.

title: How Do We Breathe? (Model Lung)
desc: The child builds a model lung from a plastic bottle and two balloons, then pulls and pushes the bottom 'diaphragm' balloon to make the inner 'lung' balloon fill and empty.
how: An adult should cut the bottle; takes 30–45 minutes.

title: Explore How Lung Infection Influences Breathing
desc: The child builds two model lungs and adds a gelatin and corn-syrup 'mucus' to one, then compares how a healthy and an 'infected' lung move air.
how: Do the basic model lung first; takes 2–3 hours including setting time.

title: Single-Celled Science: Yeasty Beasties
desc: The child puts yeast with warm water, sugar or salt into bottles topped with balloons and watches the sugar bottle's balloon inflate with gas made by living yeast.
how: Use baker's yeast from the market; links to why idli batter and bread rise.

title: Yeasty Beasties (science project)
desc: A fuller project: the child feeds yeast different additives such as sugar, salt, baking soda or vinegar in balloon-capped bottles and measures the gas produced by water displacement.
how: For an older child ready to record and compare measurements.

title: Do-It-Yourself DNA
desc: The child mashes strawberries with salt, water and dish soap, filters the mix and layers cold rubbing alcohol on top to see whitish strands of DNA they can spool on a toothpick.
how: An adult should handle the rubbing alcohol; banana works if strawberries are out of season.

title: Make Your Own Stethoscope
desc: The child makes a stethoscope from a funnel and a cardboard tube, listens to a heartbeat and counts heart rate at rest and after exercise.
how: Takes 20–30 minutes; have the child skip or run on the spot between counts.

title: How Well Do You Wash Your Hands?
desc: The child coats their hands in washable paint as pretend germs, then rinses and washes in different ways to see how much is left and learns a step-by-step scrub.
how: Under 10 minutes; a good way to make the handwashing habit stick.

title: Make a Homemade Compass
desc: The child magnetises a sewing needle by stroking it with a magnet, pushes it through a cork disc and floats it in water to watch it point north–south.
how: Supervise with the needle; a leaf can replace the cork.

title: Generate Electricity with a Lemon Battery
desc: The child makes a battery from lemons, copper coins and aluminium foil strips, and links two in series to feel a faint tingle from the current.
how: Copper coins are rare in India; a piece of bare copper wire works as the copper electrode.

title: Which Materials Conduct Electricity?
desc: The child turns a torch's parts into a tester and checks household objects such as foil, paper clips, wood, plastic and rubber; the bulb lights for conductors and stays dark for insulators.
how: Uses only torch batteries, so it is a safe way to explain why wires are covered in plastic.

title: Make a Paper Circuit
desc: The child lays copper tape on paper with a coin-cell battery and an LED to make a light-up card, seeing that a closed loop lights the LED and a break stops it.
how: Keep coin cells away from younger siblings, as they are dangerous if swallowed.

title: Squishy Circuits
desc: The child makes conductive and insulating play dough and builds dough sculptures that light up LEDs, learning which dough lets electricity flow.
how: The doughs are made from flour, salt and sugar in the kitchen.

title: Model the Rock Cycle with Crayons
desc: The child shaves old crayons, presses the shavings into a layered 'sedimentary rock', then heats and cools them to model metamorphic and igneous rocks.
how: An adult should handle the heating; takes 20–30 minutes.

title: Soil Science: Winogradsky Columns
desc: The child packs mud into a clear plastic bottle to make a Winogradsky column and watches over weeks as coloured layers of soil microbes grow.
how: A long-running project; place it near a window and keep a weekly log.

title: Clean Water and Aquifer Science
desc: The child uses popcorn kernels, cornmeal and cornstarch as different kinds of soil to model an aquifer and see how soil layers filter water.
how: Good for younger children before the bottle water-filter activity.

title: Bird-Spotting Science: Predicting a Bird's Lifestyle from its Feet
desc: The child looks closely at bird feet and tests whether foot type predicts how a bird lives, with an extension comparing beaks and what birds eat.
how: Try it with local birds such as pigeons, mynas, ducks and crows.

title: Build a Bird Feeder to Study Birds
desc: The child builds a bird feeder and uses it to watch and study the birds that visit.
how: Hang it on a balcony and keep a list of visitors through the week.

title: Can You Hide in Plain Sight?
desc: Using a pincer-grip 'beak', volunteers hunt coloured prey on different backgrounds, showing how camouflage helps some prey survive.
how: Works best with two or more players, such as siblings or a parent.

title: What Are You Blubbering About?
desc: The child coats a finger in shortening as pretend blubber and times how long it stays comfortable in ice water compared with a bare finger.
how: Ghee or vanaspati can stand in for shortening; links to animals of cold places.

title: How Do Arctic Animals Stay Warm?
desc: The child compares bags of fat, feathers and plain air in cold water to feel which insulates best, finding that feathers work by trapping air.

title: Suck It Up! How Water Moves Through Plants
desc: The child stands white flowers in coloured water and checks them over two days as the dye travels up the stem and colours the petals.
how: White chrysanthemums or tuberose work if carnations are hard to find.

title: Water Transport in Plants
desc: A lesson for Class 2–3: the child puts a white flower and a leafy celery stalk in dyed water, watches the colour rise, then cuts the celery to see the coloured tubes that carry water.
how: Follow the lesson as written; it includes the discussion questions.

title: Iron-Rich Foods: How to Get the Most Out of Them
desc: The child uses diluted and full-strength vinegar as models of a full and an empty stomach and compares how fast iron dissolves in each.
how: A science-fair-level project for an older child; read the procedure together first.

title: Fun with Static
desc: The child rubs a balloon on their hair, makes it stick to a wall or shirt, and uses it to roll an empty can or move a ping-pong ball without touching it.
how: A five-minute starter with a balloon; best on a dry day.
